sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Document parsing converts a document page into text that keeps the structure of the page, such as its headings, reading order, tables and formulas. Some documents store their text but not its structure; a born-digital PDF, for example, records characters and their positions, but not which characters form a heading or a paragraph [ 29 ] . Others, such as scanned or photographed pages, are only images. In both cases, tables, charts, formatting and formulas are among the hardest elements to recover. Parsing mistakes are costly, because retrieval systems, extraction pipelines and document agents read only the parsed text and cannot correct it [ 50 , 48 , 49 ] . For example, a value placed under the wrong column header becomes a wrong answer, although the table still looks well formed [ 48 ] . Parsing must also be fast, because training-data generation and retrieval indexing process millions of pages, and document agents need low-latency parsing to answer questions quickly. Compact document-parsing VLMs have become the standard way to parse documents, and a 1–4B parameter model that reads the page now replaces the heuristic pipelines in most open systems [ 24 , 40 , 25 , 10 , 2 ] . These models read plain text well. They are less accurate on complex tables and charts. Tables with merged cells, spanned headers or irregular shapes come out with cells in the wrong place, and long tables are often cut short or lose rows. Charts are usually treated as pictures, so most models describe them or skip them instead of writing out their data. These models are also slow. They write one token at a time, and a dense page of tables runs to thousands of tokens, so parsing thousands of pages takes hours of GPU time. We built OCRia-1 for these elements and for speed. We introduce OCRia-1 , a 4B document-parsing VLM built on Qwen3.5-4B [ 32 , 33 ] . OCRia-1 transcribes the page into Markdown, writing tables as HTML with their full structure, charts as tables of their data points, and formulas as L a T e X . OCRia-1 is more accurate on tables, charts and text formatting than every system we compare it with ( ), and its mean ParseBench score over the four dimensions we evaluate is 0.87, against 0.75 for the next-best system ( Table 3 ). It is also, to our knowledge, the fastest published document-parsing VLM. On one B200 GPU, the served model decodes at about 4,700 tokens per second with a single request and about 1,900 tokens per second per request with eight concurrent requests. With 64 concurrent requests, it parses about 10 pages per second, at no measurable cost on the benchmarks ( Section 5.3 ). We plan to make a version of OCRia-1 available. We gave priority to tables, charts and text formatting in both the data and the training. These elements carry much of the information in enterprise documents, such as financial reports, insurance filings, contracts and medical publications. Our approach is to invest in training data for these elements, in rewards that score them directly, and in inference speed. The training set has two kinds of pages ( Section 2 ). Real pages come from public document collections, chosen where document-parsing VLMs still fail, such as dense tables, tables with cells that span several rows or columns, and charts. A pipeline of proprietary vision-language models transcribes each real page, and we keep the transcription only when independent checks agree with it ( Section 2.2 ). Synthetic pages come from our own generators, which render varied page layouts together with their exact transcription. They supply what real collections do not contain in quantity, such as long tables, icon tables and rich inline formatting. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches the model to transcribe these pages, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) then rewards it for table cells placed under the right headers, chart values and formatting marks. To accelerate decoding, we use speculative decoding [ 19 , 4 ] with a block-diffusion draft model [ 5 ] , and adapt the number of draft tokens to the batch size to maintain high throughput at larger batch sizes. We also quantized OCRia-1 to four-bit NVFP4, while retaining FP8 or BF16 in layers where lower-precision quantization reduced evaluation scores. Finally, we customized vLLM with architecture-specific CUDA kernels and fused operations to improve GPU compute and memory-bandwidth utilization. This report provides more information about how we trained OCRia-1 and is organized as follows. Section 2 describes our diverse, high-quality mix of real and synthetic data, which we view as the primary driver of OCRia-1’s performance. Section 3 describes SFT and RLVR with rewards that score table cells and chart values. Section 4 describes speculative decoding, quantization and serving optimizations. Section 5 compares OCRia-1 with eight other systems on four transcription benchmarks and measures its inference speed on one B200 GPU. Section 6 places this work among other document-parsing VLMs.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: Our data is collected strategically around the most challenging aspects of document parsing, including charts and long tables or tables with many spanning cells ( Section 6 ). We developed a proprietary workflow to build a high-quality training corpus from both transcribed public documents and synthesised pages, to close the gaps that remain in public datasets. We used synthetic data to fill the gaps left by real data, which ensures the variety of hard cases needed for training. This allows us to include the long tail of difficult cases without the struggle of finding them in real data. Synthetic data comes with training ground truth by design, and we carefully designed the layouts of the synthetic examples to be as realistic as possible. This strategy ensures that the training set covers the aspects a model needs to get right, while keeping our customer data outside the training corpus. Section 2.1 describes what we collected and why. Section 2.2 describes how we generate ground truth for a real page: a teacher pipeline writes it, and independent checks decide whether we keep it. Section 2.3 describes how the synthetic pages are generated. sections.heading: Building the corpus
sections.text: We built the corpus targeting the areas where document-parsing VLMs still fail, including dense and spanned tables, mathematics, non-Latin scripts, old scans and handwriting, and charts. We iteratively refine the SFT dataset, using model evaluations to guide targeted data collection and synthesis. We retain data from earlier rounds to preserve existing capabilities. The training set has 100,979 pages, about 0.37 B target tokens: 82,943 real pages and 18,036 synthetic pages ( ≈ \approx 121 M target tokens). Real and synthetic pages share the ground-truth format shown in Section A.1 . Real pages come from eleven source families, chosen for breadth of layout and a permissible license ( Table 1 ). We collected about one million PDFs from these sources and kept the pages counted in Table 1 . To ensure diversity, we take at most three pages per document (six for table collections) and let no single source family, language or query group dominate. We use the PDF text layer to filter for pages that contain tables, charts and mathematics. Synthetic pages let us generate challenging examples at scale with exact ground truth. Long tables, for example, are hard to find in real collections and difficult to annotate accurately. Pages emphasizing each element type are produced by a dedicated generator ( Table 2 ). We ensure that the generators produce diverse formatting that still reflects what real documents look like. sections.heading: Transcribing and verifying real pages
sections.text: We use our proprietary ground truth generation workflow to produce accurate ground truth for SFT at a large scale. The workflow consists of the following steps ( Figure 1 ).

sections.heading: Teacher annotations.
sections.text: The teacher is composed of workflows to parse different complex page elements such as tables and charts, whose outputs are then combined with text predictions into the transcription of the entire page. The transcription follows the output format described in Section A.1 .

sections.heading: Annotation audit.
sections.text: Since teacher annotations might not be perfect, once the initial transcription of a page has been produced, a mid-size VLM checks that the transcription is correct with respect to the source page image using a set of auditing rules, which target different aspects of the transcription ( Section A.2 ). The rules check for various common failure modes, such as incorrect table headers and table cells holding the wrong value. When a rule fails, the VLM is called to correct the transcription, focusing on the detected issues.

sections.heading: Text layer grounding.
sections.text: For digital PDF pages in which the text content can be extracted directly, the ground truth is compared against the PDF text to ensure the completeness of the transcription. While this text layer lacks the semantic structure of the page, the ground truth needs to at least match the text for it to be correct.

sections.heading: Correction & re-evaluation.
sections.text: In correction & re-evaluation, we use a large VLM to correct the page transcription and re-evaluate the correctness of the generated ground truth. A digital PDF page is approved as ground truth when it passes both the audit and the text layer grounding; a page that fails either check, and every scanned page, goes to correction & re-evaluation ( Section A.2 ). Only when the large VLM’s validation and correction attempts fail do we route the page for human revision.

sections.heading: Generating synthetic pages
sections.text: Real documents best represent what the model will see in use. However, some of the complex document types that these models struggle with are scarce, and for others precise ground truth cannot be extracted reliably at scale. To close those gaps, we use synthetic data that follows the distribution of real documents while keeping a high diversity of styles. We developed an internal workflow that generates PDF pages from pre-synthesised ground truth: the generator samples document styles and templates from real documents while rendering that ground truth. The generators cover tables and charts, including long tables of 5k–12k tokens, spanned headers, icon cells and 28 chart types; forms and inline formatting, including checkboxes and fill-in fields; and documents shown with tracked changes ( Table 2 ). The synthetic ground truth is generated in the same format as the ground truth of the real pages ( Section A.1 ).

sections.heading: Training
sections.text: We train OCRia-1 in two stages for accurate document parsing. SFT teaches Qwen3.5-4B to transcribe document pages in our output format. RLVR addresses errors left by SFT by scoring page structure and content directly, such as table cells, chart values and formatting marks, while penalizing degenerate output such as repetition. A separate draft model accelerates inference ( Section 4 ).

sections.heading: SFT.
sections.text: We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B on 100,979 pages ( Section 2 ). We prompt the model to transcribe each page ( Appendix F ), using Markdown with HTML tables to represent its content and structure. We render each page at 1,024 px on its long side and use a 20,480-token context to accommodate long tables. Section B.1 gives the filtering and training settings; Section B.3 reports results at higher image resolutions.

sections.heading: RLVR.
sections.text: After SFT, we train the model with GRPO [ 36 , 8 ] with the goal of refining and enhancing the behaviors that the model has already learned to some extent. We also want it to improve its formatting and consistency. Our RLVR setup differs from previous work in two ways. First, it uses a larger set of rewards covering different page elements, along with additional penalties. Second, it weights the rewards dynamically according to their variance across rollouts, so that page elements that appear less often still contribute meaningfully to the update. Section B.2 gives the settings. • Training data. The stage trains on 11,234 pages ( Table 7 ). For rollout generation we keep the image at its stored resolution, mostly at or above 150 dpi ( Table 8 ). We train on the full corpus without removing pages with low GRPO advantages, as removing such pages gave mixed results ( Section B.5 ). • Reward design. Our reward function combines terms across multiple dimensions of transcription quality ( Section B.4.3 ), giving partial credit for correct aspects of imperfect outputs. Most of its thirty-four terms ( Section B.4 ) are scores, which give credit for what is right. Twelve are penalties, which are zero unless the output has the error they check for, e.g., a penalty for merged or split tables ( Section B.4.1 ). To ensure the reward function is well defined and hard to game, we test each reward term against ground truth before training ( Section B.4.2 ). • Reward weighting. We carefully weight reward terms with variance-based reweighting to balance their influence on group-relative updates. A term’s influence depends on both its weight and its variation across rollouts, so fixed weights alone can let one dimension dominate at the expense of others ( Section B.4.4 ). We also avoid normalizing each term by its own within-group statistics [ 14 ] , which can give penalties as much influence as the quality terms they are intended to protect. We train several checkpoints that are stronger in different dimensions and merge them into the final OCRia-1 model by checkpoint averaging [ 45 , 34 ] .

sections.heading: Inference
sections.text: We accelerate inference through speculative decoding, mixed-precision quantization, and optimizations to the vLLM serving runtime.

sections.heading: Speculative decoding.
sections.text: We use speculative decoding [ 19 , 4 ] for a lossless inference speedup: a small draft model proposes several tokens ahead and the full model verifies them all in one forward pass. We trained a six-layer DFlash 2 [ 5 , 15 ] block-diffusion speculator with 0.69B parameters on document pages from our training corpus. We use a block of 32 tokens, against the 8 to 16 tokens used by DFlash and by the draft of HunyuanOCR-1.5 [ 20 ] , so a verification step can produce up to 32 tokens. We implemented a dynamic draft length, using longer drafts at low concurrency to improve per-request decoding speed and shorter drafts at higher concurrency to preserve throughput as verification costs grow. With 31 draft tokens, each verification step emits an average of 12.5 to 17.5 tokens depending on the page set, including one token from the target. These averages remain consistent across evaluated batch sizes ( Table 22 ). We also refined DFlash 2’s draft-token selection with dynamic programming, slightly increasing accepted tokens per step at negligible cost. Section E.2 provides further implementation details.

sections.heading: Quantization.
sections.text: We quantize OCRia-1 to a mix of NVFP4 and FP8 [ 1 ] , while retaining BF16 for the vision encoder. We calibrate on the model’s own transcriptions and select each layer’s precision, keeping only configurations whose scores remain within measurement noise of the BF16 baseline.

sections.heading: Serving optimizations.
sections.text: We customize vLLM [ 18 ] to reduce repeated work and improve GPU utilization. Our port of ReplaySSM [ 16 ] replays accepted tokens from a saved recurrent state, avoiding a state snapshot at every draft position. We write several CUDA kernels to optimize inference. We also fuse activation and quantization operations, build batch metadata once per step, and reuse the shared prompt prefix across requests. Appendix E gives the quantization, implementation and validation details.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate OCRia-1 as a document-parsing VLM along two axes: parsing quality and serving speed. We measure parsing quality across four public benchmarks with complementary coverage, from enterprise pages and broad document layouts to cropped tables in nine languages; we measure serving speed on one B200 GPU. We first describe the benchmark scope and the evaluation protocol ( Section 5.1 ), then report parsing results ( Section 5.2 ), and finally measure inference speed ( Section 5.3 ).

sections.heading: Benchmarks and protocol
sections.text: We have considered four well-known public benchmarks. The benchmarks rely on different document distributions due to their focus, and this variety ensures a thorough evaluation of our model across a diversity of document parsing problems. Unless otherwise specified, and to ensure fair evaluation, we have evaluated OCRia-1 with the transcription prompt of Appendix F , on the same page renderings at each benchmark’s standard resolution, and scored it with the benchmark’s own scorer. Appendix D provides additional details about the evaluation protocol. The benchmarks are: • ParseBench [ 48 ] contains pages from enterprise documents such as insurance, finance and government filings, and grades text content, text formatting and charts with rules written against each page, and tables with a table-structure metric ( Appendix D ). Its fifth dimension, visual grounding, scores whether each extracted block is located, labelled and matched to its content; OCRia-1 does not output bounding boxes at this moment, so we leave that dimension out. • olmOCR-bench [ 29 ] runs 7,010 pass-or-fail unit tests on 1,403 pages, grouped into arXiv mathematics, old scans with mathematics, old scans, tables, multi-column pages, headers and footers, and long passages of small text. • PulseBench-Tab [ 31 ] scores 1,820 cropped tables in nine languages by comparing the predicted cell grid with the reference grid. • fr-bench-pdf2md [ 35 ] runs olmOCR-style tests on 721 difficult French pages.

sections.heading: Inference efficiency
sections.text: For inference speed, we use a separate comparison set of fast open-weight document-parsing VLMs, including compact models and systems with speculative decoding. On one B200, OCRia-1 leads the five evaluated systems in both decoding speed and page throughput at one and eight concurrent requests ( Figure 3 ). Its per-request decoding speed is respectively 3.4 × 3.4\times and 2.0 × 2.0\times that of the next-fastest system. In a separate concurrency sweep, OCRia-1 parses 10.21 pages per second at 64 concurrent requests, the highest concurrency tested with p90 latency below 10 s ( Table 20 ). sections.heading: Related Work
sections.text: OCRia-1 reads the whole page with one VLM, and it differs from earlier document-parsing VLMs mainly in its training data and its rewards. The document-parsing VLMs we compare against include olmOCR-2 [ 30 ] , dots.mocr [ 51 ] , LightOnOCR [ 40 , 25 ] , Chandra [ 7 ] , Infinity-Parser2-Pro [ 13 ] and Surya [ 28 ] , and other recent ones include the DeepSeek-OCR series [ 42 , 43 ] and TeleOCR [ 2 ] . Pages with correct annotations are scarce, so many training sets are labeled by a larger model or generated synthetically. These models are weakest on the page types with the fewest annotated examples, such as charts, long or heavily spanned tables, low-resource languages and scanned pages. We built our training data around these page types, and we believe this data is one of the reasons OCRia-1 outperforms the models we compare it with ( Sections 2 and 5 ). Some of these models continue training with reinforcement learning on a reward computed from the parsed output [ 41 , 30 , 40 , 13 ] . Compared to previous work, our RLVR has two main differences. The first is a larger set of rewards for different page elements and more penalties ( Section B.4.3 ). The second is a mechanism to dynamically weight the different rewards based on rollout variance ( Section B.4.4 ), which gives a higher contribution to less frequent and varied rollout elements. We combine a block-diffusion draft model with quantization and custom kernels, and we report the resulting inference performance ( Section 5.3 ). There are other models using several techniques to speed up inference, such as GLM-OCR [ 10 ] , which predicts several tokens per step, and diffusion-based models [ 26 , 9 ] , which write many tokens in parallel. Some document-parsing VLMs also use speculative decoding: HunyuanOCR-1.5 with a DFlash draft model [ 20 ] , HPD-Parsing with multi-token prediction heads [ 44 ] , and GravityOCR with drafts from the same network [ 17 ] ; Section E.2 compares how many draft tokens they accept per step with ours.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: At the time of this report, OCRia-1, a 4B document-parsing VLM, has the highest scores on tables, charts and text formatting among all the systems we compare it with ( Table 3 ), and its largest leads are on charts and text formatting in ParseBench ( Table 4 ). At ten pages per second, one GPU parses about 860,000 pages a day ( Section 5.3 ), so the training data for the next model, the backlog of a document store or the attachments a document agent receives can be parsed on one machine. We plan to make a version of OCRia-1 available soon. Most of the work for OCRia-1 went into preparing the training data. Our focus on high quality data rather than quantity is one of the reasons of OCRia-1’s performance. Synthetic pages came with ground truth from their generators, and real pages were transcribed by a multi-stage pipeline whose output we checked by rule and against the text stored in the PDF. After SFT, we trained the model with RLVR and averaged checkpoints, and a draft model significantly speeds up decoding. The same way of collecting and annotating data can be applied to prepare data for the cases where OCRia-1 currently scores lowest, such as old scans, tables in Arabic, Greek and Korean, and long tables whose rows run past the output budget ( Section D.2 ). Also, we have not yet released a model capable of predicting layout, which is left as work for a future release.

sections.text: This appendix gives the output format ( Section A.1 ) and the verification rules ( Section A.2 ) behind Section 2 .

sections.heading: Output format
sections.text:
OUTPUT FORMAT Mathematics Inline formulas use \li@chip $…$ and display formulas use \li@chip $$…$$; a printed equation number such as (3) is written as plain text after the closing \li@chip $$, not inside the formula. Tables & Charts Write each table as one line of HTML with \li@chip header cells and exact \li@chip rowspan/ \li@chip colspan spans. Cells can contain \li@chip , \li@chip , \li@chip , \li@chip
and \li@chip / \li@chip . Captions appear on the line before the table; charts are transcribed as tables. Inline formatting Use \li@chip / \li@chip tags rather than Unicode superscripts; \li@chip **bold**, \li@chip *italic*, \li@chip and \li@chip ˜˜strike˜˜ mark bold, italic, underlined and struck-through text; \li@chip
marks a printed horizontal rule. Lists and forms List items use \li@chip * at the top level and \li@chip - for nested items; checkboxes use \li@chip [x]/ \li@chip [ ], and fill-in fields use \li@chip [___]. Page furniture Place the running header on the first line in \li@chip …, the running footer on the last line in \li@chip …, and the printed page number in \li@chip … inside its header or footer. Images Write \li@chip ![label: content] without a filename: the label identifies the image type (logo, photo, chart, flowchart, …), and the content is a sentence describing a photograph, the printed words of a logo or seal, or the digits of a barcode. Signatures and seals use \li@chip [signature: Name] and \li@chip [seal: text]; an overlay watermark appears as one \li@chip line at the top. Flowcharts Place a fenced \li@chip mermaid block after the image marker.

sections.heading: Verification rules
sections.text: For a digital PDF page, the transcription is approved as ground truth if it passes both the audit and the text layer grounding; if either fails, the page is sent to correction and re-evaluation. A scanned page always goes to correction and re-evaluation, since there is no text layer to confirm the transcription. Table 5 lists the rules of the audit in Section 2.2 , by group. The audit and the reviewer answer every rule with pass, fail, uncertain or not applicable, and quote the part of the page that decided the answer. Group Rules What it catches TABLE RULES 25 rules, asked of every table Cells T01–T04 one wrapped cell split into several rows; separately printed records merged into one multi-line cell; invented spacer rows; real blank cells removed or filled Spans T05, T07–T09, T23 a category or subtotal label spanned across cells that hold values; wrong grid or span dimensions; repeated values merged into one cell; a real merged cell that loses what it covers; empty regions the rules treat as equivalent flagged as errors Headers T10–T12 header tiers flattened, dropped or made up; a header span over the wrong columns; missing or invented headers and columns Content T06, T13–T16 sparse or subsection values left out; a cell’s text or number corrupted; superscripts, footnote marks or symbols detached from their value; a value in the wrong row or column; a long table that stops early or repeats Boundaries T17–T22 a borderless grid flattened into prose; one table split at a visual band; neighbouring tables woven together; a continuation that invents row relationships; printed occurrences duplicated or suppressed; captions, notes and totals attached to the wrong table Source image T24, T25 a source image or render that is incomplete or misleading; emphasis in the source turned into table structure PAGE RULES 7 rules, asked once per page Omissions P01 text outside the tables that is missing: labels, captions, notes, headers, footers Inventions P02 invented or duplicated text, including a plausible footer number Pictures P03 a picture that is unaccounted for or given the wrong kind Reading order P04 a wrong order across columns, sidebars or right-to-left text; tables and prose out of place Ownership P05 a caption, note, total or detached cell held by the wrong block at a table boundary Character fidelity P06 a character outside the tables that differs from the print, including a printed typo that was corrected Image completeness P07 a clipped or unreadable source image, or a missing illustration SCRIPT RULES added for non-Latin pages Image markers P08, P09 a picture with no marker, two markers or the wrong class; a marker, header band or footer band that is not in the output format Script fidelity P10 an invented, dropped or substituted character; transliteration; digits converted to another numeral system (for example Arabic-Indic digits written as 0–9); a line repeated more often than it is printed Table 5: Rules of the audit. The table rules apply to every table of a draft and the page rules once to the page. The last group is added for pages in non-Latin scripts.

sections.heading: Appendix B Training
sections.text: This appendix gives the training details left out of the main text. Sections B.1 and B.2 list the SFT and RLVR settings, Section B.3 reports the experiments with the training resolution, Section B.4 lists the components of the reward, and Section B.5 reports the tests on pages that give no training signal.

sections.heading: Supervised fine-tuning settings
sections.text: The SFT context length is 20,480 tokens. Context-length filtering excludes 994 real pages from the collected corpus, leaving 100,979 pages. We keep the training recipe fixed when comparing data mixes to isolate their effects. The SFT checkpoint for OCRia-1 was trained for two epochs with AdamW at a global batch of 64 sequences, a peak learning rate of 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} , a cosine schedule with linear warm-up over 3% of the steps (94 of 3,154), and zero weight decay. Sequences use bf16 without sequence packing (each GPU processes two sequences at a time). We chose the learning rate by starting from a setting that had already worked well (batch 16, learning rate 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} ), scaling it with the square root of the batch size up to batch 64, and then keeping it fixed. We train on four nodes with eight B200 GPUs each.

sections.heading: Training resolution
sections.text: Every training page is rendered at 1,024 px on its long side, about 93 dpi and 800 image tokens for a portrait letter page, while the benchmarks serve pages at a higher resolution ( Section 5 ). We also trained at a resolution closer to the serving one, and no transcription score changed by more than about a point. We trained Qwen3.5-4B twice on a 30k-page subset of the SFT data, with the same recipe as the main runs, once with every page rendered at 1,024 px and once at 1,536 px, which gives 2.25 times the image tokens. The 1,536 px run took 1.2 times as long. Table 9 gives the scores, with every benchmark served at its usual rendering. On ParseBench and PulseBench-Tab no score changed by more than 0.01, and on olmOCR-bench the table tests rose by 0.8 points and the math tests fell by 1.5. The resolution at serving time matters far more than the resolution at training time. We served the same two models on ParseBench in two ways: at the benchmark’s standard rendering (150 dpi, about 1,650 px on the long side of a letter page) and with every page downscaled to at most 1,024 px. Downscaling cost both models about 0.08: the 1,536 px model fell from 0.83 to 0.75 and the 1,024 px model from 0.84 to 0.76. A model trained only at 1,024 px therefore still benefits from the extra image tokens of a larger page at serving time ( Appendix C ), and downscaling pages to save tokens is expensive. sections.heading: How the components are combined
sections.text: The thirty-four components are grouped into sixteen panels, and the panels into nine targets. The nine targets are a benchmark pass rate, content fidelity, table content, table structure, chart value-label keying, layout and attribution, layout boxes, formatting marks, and output hygiene. Each component k k is either a score s k s_{k} or a penalty p k p_{k} , both in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , and it contributes to the reward with its weight w k w_{k} : c k ​ ( y ) = { w k ​ s k ​ ( y ) if k is a score, − w k ​ p k ​ ( y ) if k is a penalty, c_{k}(y)=\begin{cases}\phantom{-}w_{k}\,s_{k}(y)&\text{if $k$ is a score,}\\ -w_{k}\,p_{k}(y)&\text{if $k$ is a penalty,}\end{cases} (1) where a penalty is zero when the output does not have the error that it checks for. The components of a panel P j P_{j} are added, and the panels are combined with weights ω j \omega_{j} normalised to sum to one: R ⁡ ( y ) = ∑ j = 1 16 ω j ∑ l ω l ​ ∑ k ∈ P j g k ​ ( y ) ​ c k ​ ( y ) . R(y)=\sum_{j=1}^{16}\frac{\omega_{j}}{\sum_{l}\omega_{l}}\sum_{k\in P_{j}}g_{k}(y)\,c_{k}(y). (2) A length gate multiplies the seven content scores, such as \li@chip cct and the table scores, and removes or reduces their credit when the output is much longer or much shorter than the reference or repeats itself. The \li@chip length_penalty also lowers the reward directly when the output is too long. For short outputs we use only the gate, because a penalty for short outputs can give an empty output a higher reward than an output with half of the page. In Equation 2 the gate is the factor g k g_{k} . Let n n and n ∗ n^{*} be the lengths in characters of the output and of the reference. For \li@chip bench, \li@chip cct, \li@chip table_align, \li@chip table_teds, \li@chip table_grits, \li@chip table_grits_trm and \li@chip chart_keying, g k g_{k} is the product g over ​ g under ​ g rep g_{\mathrm{over}}\,g_{\mathrm{under}}\,g_{\mathrm{rep}} , and for every other component it is one. sections.heading: Tests for reward terms
sections.text: Every reward term is tested on constructed answers before training. The tests led to three rules for writing a reward term. A component with nothing to compare must return zero, because returning a fixed middle score instead gave an empty answer a quarter of the summed score. A check on order must require content, because an empty sequence is trivially in order and would otherwise score well on reading order. A check on counts or labels must require correct placement, because otherwise an answer with every element in the wrong place still scores well.

sections.heading: How the reward compares
sections.text: The document-parsing VLMs that add a reinforcement-learning stage use similar algorithms and differ mainly in what their rewards score. Table 12 places ours beside them, using each system’s own account of its reward. Beyond covering more of the page, our reward differs in how finely it scores and in its penalties. An edit-distance reward is smooth, but it is computed over the whole page and cannot say which cell of a table is wrong. A binary unit test says exactly what it checks and gives nothing in between, so a nearly correct table and an absent one are worth the same. Infinity-Parser2 grades cropped tables with tree edit distance, but it scores a full page with an edit distance. Our terms are graded where a partial parse deserves partial credit, and binary where a page either carries a parseable table or does not. Twelve of our thirty-four components are penalties. A reward built only from scores costs an output nothing for repeating itself, running past the end of the page or carrying formatting the page does not have. Two of the published rewards guard against repetition. olmOCR 2 rewards an output that ends with the end-of-sequence token, and LightOnOCR penalises repetition loops. None of them describes penalties for split or merged tables, unfinished tables or formatting the page does not have. Our reward needs the formatting penalty because the formatting tests measure recall alone, so without it, styling every line raises the score. sections.heading: Balancing the terms.
sections.text: In a group-relative update, the influence of a term depends on how much it varies within the group as well as on its weight. A term with a small weight and a large variance can therefore dominate the gradient, while a term that barely varies, such as the content term, rarely decides the ranking. In one training run, the formatting term became the largest single contribution to the ranking within ten steps, the contribution of the table term fell by half, and the table scores regressed. Normalising the panel weights to sum to one also lowers the weight of every other panel when one target is split into two panels, and giving the formula term its own panel cut its effective weight by a factor of four. The published remedy is to normalise each component by its own within-group statistics before summing [ 14 ] , but it did not work for our reward. Several of our components are one-sided guardrails, penalties that are zero when nothing is wrong, and normalising them to unit variance gives them as much influence as the terms they protect; on stored groups, it moved a share of the gradient onto them. In a training run with this normalisation, the policy removed formatting markup to avoid the formatting penalty, the formatting score collapsed and the overall score fell with it. A revised normalisation leaves the guardrails out of the normalised set, puts a floor on the within-group standard deviation, clips the normalised score and blends the result with the ordinary advantage of the weighted reward. On the same stored groups, it removes the guardrails’ share of the gradient and raises the share of the chart and table terms, and Constrained GRPO [ 11 ] independently argues for combining standardised advantages over standardising a scalarised reward. We have tested it only offline, and OCRia-1 is not trained with it. Reweighting moves gradient between objectives but cannot add signal, so a chart page on which every rollout fails in the same way gives no signal with any weights. Because the gradients of the objectives are correlated, projecting one gradient out of another [ 47 ] also changes the others.

sections.heading: Pages with no training signal
sections.text: Published remedies for pages whose rollouts agree are to filter batches by disagreement [ 46 ] , to select prompts by their effect on learning [ 22 ] , and to schedule difficulty as the model improves [ 38 , 6 ] . We report results for two of them.

sections.heading: Filtering during training.
sections.text: We filtered batches by disagreement on one objective. This increased that objective’s share of the gradient but reduced the signal for the other objectives. The filter reads the current policy’s own disagreement, which changes as the policy changes.

sections.heading: Selecting the pages before training.
sections.text: This test removes, before training starts, the pages that the SFT model is unlikely to learn from. We sampled each candidate page eight times with the SFT model and set aside the 6,096 pages whose samples agreed. The SFT model had already transcribed 4,713 of them correctly and was uniformly poor on 1,215. On the remaining 168, the agreement came from a suspect reference. A page that the SFT model already transcribes is unlikely to divide the policy trained from it, so these pages are the least likely to carry signal later. Training on the remaining pages stayed ahead of the full corpus at both steps we measured, by a margin that narrowed, and the two runs improved on different dimensions. OCRia-1 is trained on the full corpus, because removing these pages gave mixed results ( Section 3 ), and the corpus still contains 3,473 of them.

sections.text: On the base model, fine-tuning only the projector raised probe accuracy by 0.08 and dropped olmOCR-bench from 71.0 to 48.0, so we did not adopt it.

sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: Every benchmark number is a single run with greedy decoding. Every measurement is on the 4B model except the projector retraining, which was run on the base model.

sections.heading: Appendix D Evaluation details
sections.text: This appendix gives the protocol of the evaluation in Section 5 , the results for each benchmark ( Section D.1 ) and the cases where the scores are lowest ( Section D.2 ).

sections.heading: Transcription benchmarks.
sections.text: ParseBench [ 48 ] grades a page on text content, text formatting, tables and charts. Text content, text formatting and charts are scored as the pass rate of rules written against the page, and tables with the combination of GriTS and TableRecordMatch (GTRM); we report the mean of the four. Pages are rendered at 300 dpi, and the model’s image processor scales a letter page down to about 4.1 megapixels, about 210 dpi. olmOCR-bench [ 29 ] holds 1,403 pages and 7,010 unit tests (a string present or absent, two strings in order, a cell under its header, an equation rendering to the same symbols), rendered at 1,288 px on the long side and scored as the mean over its seven categories and the baseline test. PulseBench-Tab [ 31 ] holds 1,820 cropped tables in nine languages scored by the T-LAG grid metric. We send the crop capped at 2,560 px with a 16k-token budget, score the largest HTML table in the answer, and report the share of tables scored, since the protocol leaves tables without a parseable prediction out of the mean. fr-bench-pdf2md [ 35 ] holds 721 difficult French pages with 2,318 olmOCR-style tests, scored as the pass rate over all of them. We render its pages at 2,048 px on the long side.

sections.heading: Post-processing.
sections.text: The model is trained on our output format ( Section A.1 ), which includes constructs that these benchmarks neither expect nor score, such as page headers and footers inside their own tags, a watermark tag, an image marker with a label, a Mermaid block for a diagram, and a horizontal rule for a printed one. Before scoring we remove these constructs from every candidate and normalize the markup inside table cells (emphasis, checkboxes, and superscripts and subscripts written back as the glyphs the page prints).

sections.heading: Rendering resolution.
sections.text: We serve each benchmark at its own standard rendering: olmOCR-bench pages at 1,288 px on the long side (about 1,240 image tokens for a letter page), and ParseBench pages at 300 dpi, which the image processor scales down to about 3,900 image tokens for a letter page. Both are above the 1,024 px, about 800 image tokens, that the model is trained on. Scores depend on this choice. With no change to the weights, giving the OCRia-1 model 2,451 image tokens per page instead of 1,240 raises its olmOCR-bench score by 2.4 points ( Appendix C ). Other models respond the same way. Chandra-OCR-2 and LightOnOCR-3 improve by 2 points on olmOCR-bench when their pages are rendered at 212 dpi. A difference of 2–3 points between two systems can come from rendering alone, so we use each benchmark’s standard rendering for the systems we evaluate ourselves. On olmOCR-bench the other systems scored much lower at our rendering, so we report their published numbers and run OCRia-1 at the standard 1,288 px. Table 17 combines our runs at 1,288 px with published scores for Mistral OCR 4.1 and olmOCR-2.

sections.heading: Other systems.
sections.text: On ParseBench, PulseBench-Tab and fr-bench-pdf2md every other system is run by us at the same renderings and scored by the same scorers. All open models (Infinity-Parser2-Pro, LightOnOCR-3-4B, Chandra-OCR-2, dots.mocr, LightOnOCR-2-1B) are served with vLLM at each model’s own image budget. LightOnOCR-3-4B runs in its grounding mode, which scores higher than its plain transcription mode on tables and charts (0.75 against 0.61 on ParseBench). olmOCR-2 runs through its own pipeline, which renders the pages itself at the size we pass. Surya OCR 2 runs through its own package, on vLLM. Where a system labels page headers, footers and pictures, those blocks are dropped the way our own tags are, and pipe tables are converted to HTML where a scorer wants HTML.

sections.heading: Areas for improvement
sections.text: The scores are lowest on the hardest cases within the areas we worked on. Old scans are the weakest olmOCR-bench category, 48.9% for OCRia-1 against 81.4 to 99.9% for the other seven categories. The other systems in Table 16 score 41.8 to 58.2% on old scans, so these pages remain hard for current document-parsing VLMs. Tables in Arabic, Greek and Korean score 0.70 to 0.77 on PulseBench-Tab, against 0.86 to 0.90 for French, Chinese, Spanish, Russian and English. Text formatting is the lowest of the four ParseBench dimensions for OCRia-1, although its 0.83 is the highest score on that dimension in Table 4 . Within it, bold passes 77% of its rules and italics 63%. Highlighting passes 35% and strikethrough 45%, and both are rare on real pages. Figures 10 and 11 show two pages at the limits of the current model.

sections.heading: Appendix E Serving stack
sections.text: This appendix describes the serving stack of Section 4 , how its speed is measured ( Section E.1 ) and the draft model ( Section E.2 ). The served model is the bf16 checkpoint quantized to a mixed NVFP4 and FP8 map [ 1 ] , calibrated on the model’s own transcriptions and chosen by a per-layer search that kept only maps within the noise of the bf16 model on ParseBench ( − 0.0039 -0.0039 , 95 % interval [ − 0.0083 , + 0.0006 ] [-0.0083,+0.0006] on 1,578 documents), with the vision encoder left in bf16. It runs on vLLM [ 18 ] with the draft of Section 4 and five changes: • a port of ReplaySSM [ 16 ] , which keeps one checkpoint of each gated-delta-network state and replays the accepted tokens instead of snapshotting the state at every draft position, with its verify kernel rewritten in CUDA; • fused activation-quantization kernels; • the batch metadata built once per step instead of once per cache group; • the prompt prefix shared by every request, captured once and injected per request; • a draft length that switches from 31 tokens to 15 above thirteen concurrent requests, where the verify step becomes compute-bound. Every change was kept only if its kernels produced the same bits as the ones they replaced or its ParseBench score on 749 documents stayed within the noise of the previous served model.

sections.heading: Speculator
sections.text: This appendix gives the details of the draft model of Section 4 . Like other recent drafts [ 3 , 23 , 12 ] it reads the hidden states the target computed for the context rather than the context’s tokens: DFlash concatenates them from eight of the target’s layers, projects them and injects them as precomputed keys and values into every draft layer, and the draft writes a whole block of tokens in one pass, with mask tokens standing in for the block positions. The convolution lets each block position see the ones before it, and the selector keeps the sixteen most likely tokens at each position, scores every pair of consecutive candidates with a low-rank bilinear term, and walks one path through the block.

sections.heading: Training details.
sections.text: The training features are the target’s hidden states at the eight layers, captured once by running the quantized target of the time over training pages with greedy decoding and the image-only transcription prompt; the target stays frozen, and the served draft was trained against the checkpoint that preceded the released one. Training has two phases and then the selector. First only the projection, its normalisation and the convolutions are trained, 72 M of the 686 M parameters, with the cross-entropy of the target’s greedy tokens weighted by exp ( − position / 4 ) \exp(-\mathrm{position}/4) , because the early positions decide whether a step accepts anything at all; on 16,384 pages this takes about ten hours on one B200 and raises the accepted length on held-out replay from 8.2 to 13.0 tokens per block. Then the whole draft is unfrozen and trained on 15,481 pages (18,142 steps on eight B200s, about four hours), warm-starting through 2k- and 8k-page stages; at equal data the unfrozen draft beats the frozen one (10.15 against 9.93 accepted tokens). The selector is fitted last on the frozen draft from its cached features, with a prefix cross-entropy over the sixteen candidates at 32 anchor positions per page, so the quantity optimized is the length of the prefix the target will accept in one verification step; it raises the held-out accepted length from 12.65 to 14.87 tokens, and more pages helped at every stage (10.2, 11.2 and 12.7 accepted tokens from 1k, 4k and 16k pages).

sections.text: We refine DFlash 2’s draft-token selection with dynamic programming. DFlash 2 greedily selects among sixteen candidates per position using scores conditioned on the previous choice. We normalise these scores into transition probabilities P i ​ ( c i ∣ c i − 1 ) P_{i}(c_{i}\mid c_{i-1}) , the probability that the target accepts candidate c i c_{i} at position i i after c i − 1 c_{i-1} , and select the chain c 1 , … , c K c_{1},\dots,c_{K} that maximises the expected accepted-prefix length: 𝔼 ⁡ [ accepted length ] = ∑ l = 1 K ∏ i ≤ l P i ​ ( c i ∣ c i − 1 ) , \mathbb{E}[\text{accepted length}]=\sum_{l=1}^{K}\prod_{i\leq l}P_{i}(c_{i}\mid c_{i-1}), (7) where c 0 c_{0} is the last verified token. Solving this objective exactly adds negligible cost and gives slightly more accepted tokens per step than the default greedy selection ( Figure 5 ).

sections.heading: Appendix F Prompts
sections.text: This is the system prompt for transcription. ⬇ Transcribe this Page in markdown , be as accurate as possible in your transcription , do not describe / summarize . Formatting : - Use ** for bold text and * for italic text . - Use ~~ text ~~ for strikethrough text . Only use this for text that is visually stricken through . - Use < mark > and </ mark > tags for highlighted text , aka text to wich a stabilo hilight was applied Only use to hilight sentence or words , not full block of text / tables . Use HTML color names for different colors of highlight , e . g . < mark style =" background - color : blue "> text </ mark >. Do not use mark for first cell of a table , as it is often used for the header and should not be highlighted . - Use < u > and </ u > tags for underlined text . - Use \* for bullet points and - for sub - bullets . - Use > for blockquotes . - Use ‘ for inline code . - Use “‘ for code blocks . - Use [ ] for empty checkboxes . - Use [ x ] for checked checkboxes . - Use < sub > and </ sub > for subscript text . - Use < sup > and </ sup > for superscript text . - Use [ ___ ] for empty fields to fill , if the field is already filled , represent them as field content in markdown . - Use $ … $ for inline equations and $$ … $$ for display equations . Do NOT use \(…\) or \[…\] — the corpus uses dollar delimiters (43,604 inline occurrences against 35 in the parenthesis form ). - Chemical formulas are NOT LaTeX : write them as plain text with < sub > and < sup >, e . g . K < sub >3</ sub > Fe ( CN )< sub >6</ sub > and 2 H < sub >2</ sub > O , never $K_3Fe ( CN ) _6$ . Reserve $ … $ for real mathematics . Tables : - Output tables in HTML when possible . - Table should not be use for page formatting ( column or grid like layout ), but only for tabular data . - Some table may be irregular , with merged cells , missing cells , or inconsistent formatting , or have an exotic structure ( like a triangular table ). Do your best to represent the table accurately with correct reading order . Charts , Graphs , and Figures : - IMPORTANT : Every chart or graph MUST be converted into an HTML < table >. This is non - negotiable . The table represent the chart data , not the chart layout . Focus on accurately capturing the underlying data and relationships in the table format . - FORBIDDEN outputs for charts : < iframe >, < embed >, < canvas >, < img >, < object >, links , URLs , or plain - text descriptions . Using any of these for a chart is an automatic FAIL . - MERMAID FALLBACK : For diagrams , figures and flowcharts that are better represented as a graph than as a table ( architecture diagrams , flowcharts , org charts , entity relationships ), use Mermaid syntax INSTEAD of an HTML table and output it between “‘ mermaid and “‘ tags . This exception applies ONLY to diagrams ; a chart or graph plotting data values is still an HTML < table >. Images : - Transcribe any text printed inside the image as markdown . - Reference the image itself as ![ label : description ], where label is exactly one of : logo , icon , photo , illustration , screenshot , map , signature , seal , code , drawing , image . Use the caption or wording the page itself prints for the description ; do not invent one , and do not describe an image the page says nothing about . Page furniture : - Output the page header ( if any ) between < page_header > and </ page_header > tags . - Output the page footer ( if any ) between < page_footer > and </ page_footer > tags . - Output the printed page number ( if any ) between < page_number > and </ page_number > tags , nested inside the header or footer band it sits in . Watermarks : - Output a watermark stamped across the page ( DRAFT , OBSOLETE , CONFIDENTIAL ) between < watermark > and </ watermark > tags , not as body text . Multi - column Text : - Unroll multi - column text into a single column format . Completeness : - Ensure ALL content from the page is transcribed without omissions . - As this is a transcription task , fidelity is of upmost importance . You should NEVER truncate or shorten tabular data . Any instance of table data that looks like "[… table data continues in rows n - m …]" or omits rows or columns will result in an automatic FAIL . Accuracy : - Maintain text and formatting as close to the original as possible within the constraints of Markdown syntax . Handwriting / Cursive Text : - If the page contains handwriting or cursive text , ignore the OCR output for those sections and rely solely on the screenshot to transcribe that content . Output result between “‘ markdown and “‘

AcostaPierre-Loïc DoulcetSimon Suo amanrangapur@gmail.com , {antonio, daniel, simon}@runllama.ai core contributors · corresponding author Introduction Document parsing converts a document page into text that keeps the structure of the page, such as its headings, reading order, tables and formulas. Some documents store their text but not its structure; a born-digital PDF, for example, records characters and their positions, but not which characters form a heading or a paragraph [ 29 ] . Others, such as scanned or photographed pages, are only images. In both cases, tables, charts, formatting and formulas are among the hardest elements to recover. Parsing mistakes are costly, because retrieval systems, extraction pipelines and document agents read only the parsed text and cannot correct it [ 50 , 48 , 49 ] . For example, a value placed under the wrong column header becomes a wrong answer, although the table still looks well formed [ 48 ] . Parsing must also be fast, because training-data generation and retrieval indexing process millions of pages, and document agents need low-latency parsing to answer questions quickly. Compact document-parsing VLMs have become the standard way to parse documents, and a 1–4B parameter model that reads the page now replaces the heuristic pipelines in most open systems [ 24 , 40 , 25 , 10 , 2 ] . These models read plain text well. They are less accurate on complex tables and charts. Tables with merged cells, spanned headers or irregular shapes come out with cells in the wrong place, and long tables are often cut short or lose rows. Charts are usually treated as pictures, so most models describe them or skip them instead of writing out their data. These models are also slow. They write one token at a time, and a dense page of tables runs to thousands of tokens, so parsing thousands of pages takes hours of GPU time. We built OCRia-1 for these elements and for speed. We introduce OCRia-1 , a 4B document-parsing VLM built on Qwen3.5-4B [ 32 , 33 ] . OCRia-1 transcribes the page into Markdown, writing tables as HTML with their full structure, charts as tables of their data points, and formulas as L a T e X . OCRia-1 is more accurate on tables, charts and text formatting than every system we compare it with ( ), and its mean ParseBench score over the four dimensions we evaluate is 0.87, against 0.75 for the next-best system ( Table 3 ). It is also, to our knowledge, the fastest published document-parsing VLM. On one B200 GPU, the served model decodes at about 4,700 tokens per second with a single request and about 1,900 tokens per second per request with eight concurrent requests. With 64 concurrent requests, it parses about 10 pages per second, at no measurable cost on the benchmarks ( Section 5.3 ). We plan to make a version of OCRia-1 available. We gave priority to tables, charts and text formatting in both the data and the training. These elements carry much of the information in enterprise documents, such as financial reports, insurance filings, contracts and medical publications. Our approach is to invest in training data for these elements, in rewards that score them directly, and in inference speed. The training set has two kinds of pages ( Section 2 ). Real pages come from public document collections, chosen where document-parsing VLMs still fail, such as dense tables, tables with cells that span several rows or columns, and charts. A pipeline of proprietary vision-language models transcribes each real page, and we keep the transcription only when independent checks agree with it ( Section 2.2 ). Synthetic pages come from our own generators, which render varied page layouts together with their exact transcription. They supply what real collections do not contain in quantity, such as long tables, icon tables and rich inline formatting. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches the model to transcribe these pages, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) then rewards it for table cells placed under the right headers, chart values and formatting marks. To accelerate decoding, we use speculative decoding [ 19 , 4 ] with a block-diffusion draft model [ 5 ] , and adapt the number of draft tokens to the batch size to maintain high throughput at larger batch sizes. We also quantized OCRia-1 to four-bit NVFP4, while retaining FP8 or BF16 in layers where lower-precision quantization reduced evaluation scores. Finally, we customized vLLM with architecture-specific CUDA kernels and fused operations to improve GPU compute and memory-bandwidth utilization. This report provides more information about how we trained OCRia-1 and is organized as follows. Section 2 describes our diverse, high-quality mix of real and synthetic data, which we view as the primary driver of OCRia-1’s performance. Section 3 describes SFT and RLVR with rewards that score table cells and chart values. Section 4 describes speculative decoding, quantization and serving optimizations. Section 5 compares OCRia-1 with eight other systems on four transcription benchmarks and measures its inference speed on one B200 GPU. Section 6 places this work among other document-parsing VLMs. Data Our data is collected strategically around the most challenging aspects of document parsing, including charts and long tables or tables with many spanning cells ( Section 6 ). We developed a proprietary workflow to build a high-quality training corpus from both transcribed public documents and synthesised pages, to close the gaps that remain in public datasets. We used synthetic data to fill the gaps left by real data, which ensures the variety of hard cases needed for training. This allows us to include the long tail of difficult cases without the struggle of finding them in real data. Synthetic data comes with training ground truth by design, and we carefully designed the layouts of the synthetic examples to be as realistic as possible. This strategy ensures that the training set covers the aspects a model needs to get right, while keeping our customer data outside the training corpus. Section 2.1 describes what we collected and why. Section 2.2 describes how we generate ground truth for a real page: a teacher pipeline writes it, and independent checks decide whether we keep it. Section 2.3 describes how the synthetic pages are generated. REAL PAGES SYNTHETIC PAGES Real-world diversity Hard cases with exact targets Collect real pages Languages, layouts, scans, handwriting Transcribe Read tables, charts and text Independent checks Image + PDF text; correct errors Generate hard cases Long tables and spanned headers Render pages Styles from real documents Page image Exact transcription Training pairs + Page image Transcription Figure 1: How the training set is built. For real pages, we generate transcriptions, check them against the page image and available PDF text, and correct errors before accepting them as ground truth. For synthetic pages, we generate the content first and render it using styles from real documents, so the correct transcription is already known. Building the corpus We built the corpus targeting the areas where document-parsing VLMs still fail, including dense and spanned tables, mathematics, non-Latin scripts, old scans and handwriting, and charts. We iteratively refine the SFT dataset, using model evaluations to guide targeted data collection and synthesis. We retain data from earlier rounds to preserve existing capabilities. The training set has 100,979 pages, about 0.37 B target tokens: 82,943 real pages and 18,036 synthetic pages ( ≈ \approx 121 M target tokens). Real and synthetic pages share the ground-truth format shown in Section A.1 . Real pages come from eleven source families, chosen for breadth of layout and a permissible license ( Table 1 ). We collected about one million PDFs from these sources and kept the pages counted in Table 1 . To ensure diversity, we take at most three pages per document (six for table collections) and let no single source family, language or query group dominate. We use the PDF text layer to filter for pages that contain tables, charts and mathematics. Synthetic pages let us generate challenging examples at scale with exact ground truth. Long tables, for example, are hard to find in real collections and difficult to annotate accurately. Pages emphasizing each element type are produced by a dedicated generator ( Table 2 ). We ensure that the generators produce diverse formatting that still reflects what real documents look like. Transcribing and verifying real pages We use our proprietary ground truth generation workflow to produce accurate ground truth for SFT at a large scale. The workflow consists of the following steps ( Figure 1 ). Teacher annotations. The teacher is composed of workflows to parse different complex page elements such as tables and charts, whose outputs are then combined with text predictions into the transcription of the entire page. The transcription follows the output format described in Section A.1 . Annotation audit. Since teacher annotations might not be perfect, once the initial transcription of a page has been produced, a mid-size VLM checks that the transcription is correct with respect to the source page image using a set of auditing rules, which target different aspects of the transcription ( Section A.2 ). The rules check for various common failure modes, such as incorrect table headers and table cells holding the wrong value. When a rule fails, the VLM is called to correct the transcription, focusing on the detected issues. Text layer grounding. For digital PDF pages in which the text content can be extracted directly, the ground truth is compared against the PDF text to ensure the completeness of the transcription. While this text layer lacks the semantic structure of the page, the ground truth needs to at least match the text for it to be correct. Correction & re-evaluation. In correction & re-evaluation, we use a large VLM to correct the page transcription and re-evaluate the correctness of the generated ground truth. A digital PDF page is approved as ground truth when it passes both the audit and the text layer grounding; a page that fails either check, and every scanned page, goes to correction & re-evaluation ( Section A.2 ). Only when the large VLM’s validation and correction attempts fail do we route the page for human revision. Generating synthetic pages Real documents best represent what the model will see in use. However, some of the complex document types that these models struggle with are scarce, and for others precise ground truth cannot be extracted reliably at scale. To close those gaps, we use synthetic data that follows the distribution of real documents while keeping a high diversity of styles. We developed an internal workflow that generates PDF pages from pre-synthesised ground truth: the generator samples document styles and templates from real documents while rendering that ground truth. The generators cover tables and charts, including long tables of 5k–12k tokens, spanned headers, icon cells and 28 chart types; forms and inline formatting, including checkboxes and fill-in fields; and documents shown with tracked changes ( Table 2 ). The synthetic ground truth is generated in the same format as the ground truth of the real pages ( Section A.1 ). Training We train OCRia-1 in two stages for accurate document parsing. SFT teaches Qwen3.5-4B to transcribe document pages in our output format. RLVR addresses errors left by SFT by scoring page structure and content directly, such as table cells, chart values and formatting marks, while penalizing degenerate output such as repetition. A separate draft model accelerates inference ( Section 4 ). SFT. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B on 100,979 pages ( Section 2 ). We prompt the model to transcribe each page ( Appendix F ), using Markdown with HTML tables to represent its content and structure. We render each page at 1,024 px on its long side and use a 20,480-token context to accommodate long tables. Section B.1 gives the filtering and training settings; Section B.3 reports results at higher image resolutions. RLVR. After SFT, we train the model with GRPO [ 36 , 8 ] with the goal of refining and enhancing the behaviors that the model has already learned to some extent. We also want it to improve its formatting and consistency. Our RLVR setup differs from previous work in two ways. First, it uses a larger set of rewards covering different page elements, along with additional penalties. Second, it weights the rewards dynamically according to their variance across rollouts, so that page elements that appear less often still contribute meaningfully to the update. Section B.2 gives the settings. • Training data. The stage trains on 11,234 pages ( Table 7 ). For rollout generation we keep the image at its stored resolution, mostly at or above 150 dpi ( Table 8 ). We train on the full corpus without removing pages with low GRPO advantages, as removing such pages gave mixed results ( Section B.5 ). • Reward design. Our reward function combines terms across multiple dimensions of transcription quality ( Section B.4.3 ), giving partial credit for correct aspects of imperfect outputs. Most of its thirty-four terms ( Section B.4 ) are scores, which give credit for what is right. Twelve are penalties, which are zero unless the output has the error they check for, e.g., a penalty for merged or split tables ( Section B.4.1 ). To ensure the reward function is well defined and hard to game, we test each reward term against ground truth before training ( Section B.4.2 ). • Reward weighting. We carefully weight reward terms with variance-based reweighting to balance their influence on group-relative updates. A term’s influence depends on both its weight and its variation across rollouts, so fixed weights alone can let one dimension dominate at the expense of others ( Section B.4.4 ). We also avoid normalizing each term by its own within-group statistics [ 14 ] , which can give penalties as much influence as the quality terms they are intended to protect. We train several checkpoints that are stronger in different dimensions and merge them into the final OCRia-1 model by checkpoint averaging [ 45 , 34 ] . Inference We accelerate inference through speculative decoding, mixed-precision quantization, and optimizations to the vLLM serving runtime. Speculative decoding. We use speculative decoding [ 19 , 4 ] for a lossless inference speedup: a small draft model proposes several tokens ahead and the full model verifies them all in one forward pass. We trained a six-layer DFlash 2 [ 5 , 15 ] block-diffusion speculator with 0.69B parameters on document pages from our training corpus. We use a block of 32 tokens, against the 8 to 16 tokens used by DFlash and by the draft of HunyuanOCR-1.5 [ 20 ] , so a verification step can produce up to 32 tokens. We implemented a dynamic draft length, using longer drafts at low concurrency to improve per-request decoding speed and shorter drafts at higher concurrency to preserve throughput as verification costs grow. With 31 draft tokens, each verification step emits an average of 12.5 to 17.5 tokens depending on the page set, including one token from the target. These averages remain consistent across evaluated batch sizes ( Table 22 ). We also refined DFlash 2’s draft-token selection with dynamic programming, slightly increasing accepted tokens per step at negligible cost. Section E.2 provides further implementation details. Quantization. We quantize OCRia-1 to a mix of NVFP4 and FP8 [ 1 ] , while retaining BF16 for the vision encoder. We calibrate on the model’s own transcriptions and select each layer’s precision, keeping only configurations whose scores remain within measurement noise of the BF16 baseline. Serving optimizations. We customize vLLM [ 18 ] to reduce repeated work and improve GPU utilization. Our port of ReplaySSM [ 16 ] replays accepted tokens from a saved recurrent state, avoiding a state snapshot at every draft position. We write several CUDA kernels to optimize inference. We also fuse activation and quantization operations, build batch metadata once per step, and reuse the shared prompt prefix across requests. Appendix E gives the quantization, implementation and validation details. Evaluation We evaluate OCRia-1 as a document-parsing VLM along two axes: parsing quality and serving speed. We measure parsing quality across four public benchmarks with complementary coverage, from enterprise pages and broad document layouts to cropped tables in nine languages; we measure serving speed on one B200 GPU. We first describe the benchmark scope and the evaluation protocol ( Section 5.1 ), then report parsing results ( Section 5.2 ), and finally measure inference speed ( Section 5.3 ). Benchmarks and protocol We have considered four well-known public benchmarks. The benchmarks rely on different document distributions due to their focus, and this variety ensures a thorough evaluation of our model across a diversity of document parsing problems. Unless otherwise specified, and to ensure fair evaluation, we have evaluated OCRia-1 with the transcription prompt of Appendix F , on the same page renderings at each benchmark’s standard resolution, and scored it with the benchmark’s own scorer. Appendix D provides additional details about the evaluation protocol. The benchmarks are: • ParseBench [ 48 ] contains pages from enterprise documents such as insurance, finance and government filings, and grades text content, text formatting and charts with rules written against each page, and tables with a table-structure metric ( Appendix D ). Its fifth dimension, visual grounding, scores whether each extracted block is located, labelled and matched to its content; OCRia-1 does not output bounding boxes at this moment, so we leave that dimension out. • olmOCR-bench [ 29 ] runs 7,010 pass-or-fail unit tests on 1,403 pages, grouped into arXiv mathematics, old scans with mathematics, old scans, tables, multi-column pages, headers and footers, and long passages of small text. • PulseBench-Tab [ 31 ] scores 1,820 cropped tables in nine languages by comparing the predicted cell grid with the reference grid. • fr-bench-pdf2md [ 35 ] runs olmOCR-style tests on 721 difficult French pages. Related Work OCRia-1 reads the whole page with one VLM, and it differs from earlier document-parsing VLMs mainly in its training data and its rewards. The document-parsing VLMs we compare against include olmOCR-2 [ 30 ] , dots.mocr [ 51 ] , LightOnOCR [ 40 , 25 ] , Chandra [ 7 ] , Infinity-Parser2-Pro [ 13 ] and Surya [ 28 ] , and other recent ones include the DeepSeek-OCR series [ 42 , 43 ] and TeleOCR [ 2 ] . Pages with correct annotations are scarce, so many training sets are labeled by a larger model or generated synthetically. These models are weakest on the page types with the fewest annotated examples, such as charts, long or heavily spanned tables, low-resource languages and scanned pages. We built our training data around these page types, and we believe this data is one of the reasons OCRia-1 outperforms the models we compare it with ( Sections 2 and 5 ). Some of these models continue training with reinforcement learning on a reward computed from the parsed output [ 41 , 30 , 40 , 13 ] . Compared to previous work, our RLVR has two main differences. The first is a larger set of rewards for different page elements and more penalties ( Section B.4.3 ). The second is a mechanism to dynamically weight the different rewards based on rollout variance ( Section B.4.4 ), which gives a higher contribution to less frequent and varied rollout elements. We combine a block-diffusion draft model with quantization and custom kernels, and we report the resulting inference performance ( Section 5.3 ). There are other models using several techniques to speed up inference, such as GLM-OCR [ 10 ] , which predicts several tokens per step, and diffusion-based models [ 26 , 9 ] , which write many tokens in parallel. Some document-parsing VLMs also use speculative decoding: HunyuanOCR-1.5 with a DFlash draft model [ 20 ] , HPD-Parsing with multi-token prediction heads [ 44 ] , and GravityOCR with drafts from the same network [ 17 ] ; Section E.2 compares how many draft tokens they accept per step with ours. Conclusion and Future Work At the time of this report, OCRia-1, a 4B document-parsing VLM, has the highest scores on tables, charts and text formatting among all the systems we compare it with ( Table 3 ), and its largest leads are on charts and text formatting in ParseBench ( Table 4 ). At ten pages per second, one GPU parses about 860,000 pages a day ( Section 5.3 ), so the training data for the next model, the backlog of a document store or the attachments a document agent receives can be parsed on one machine. We plan to make a version of OCRia-1 available soon. Most of the work for OCRia-1 went into preparing the training data. Our focus on high quality data rather than quantity is one of the reasons of OCRia-1’s performance. Synthetic pages came with ground truth from their generators, and real pages were transcribed by a multi-stage pipeline whose output we checked by rule and against the text stored in the PDF. After SFT, we trained the model with RLVR and averaged checkpoints, and a draft model significantly speeds up decoding. The same way of collecting and annotating data can be applied to prepare data for the cases where OCRia-1 currently scores lowest, such as old scans, tables in Arabic, Greek and Korean, and long tables whose rows run past the output budget ( Section D.2 ). Also, we have not yet released a model capable of predicting layout, which is left as work for a future release.
